problem: It says 'fatigue of plates under repeated bending'. Link plates are not bent in service; they carry a fluctuating tensile load as the chain goes round, so the standard failure mode is tensile fatigue of the link plates (plus impact fatigue of rollers and bushes). A student will write 'bending fatigue of plates' in the exam.
fix: Write: fatigue of the link plates under the fluctuating tension, and impact fatigue of rollers and bushes at each engagement with the sprocket.

problem: It says round up to an even number of links 'and shorten the centre distance'. Rounding L up from 107.5 to 108 pitches means the same sprockets must sit further apart, not closer: with L = 108 the exact centre distance is about 503 mm, not less than 500 mm. Shortening the centre distance would leave the chain slack.
fix: Say: round up to an even number of links, then recompute the exact centre distance for that link count (it comes out slightly larger, about 3 mm more here), or keep C and take up the small extra slack with an idler or by moving the motor.

problem: 'wear of pins, bushes and rollers, which increases pitch' lumps the roller in. Pitch is the pin-centre distance; only pin and bush wear stretch the chain. Roller wear reduces the roller diameter and damages the tooth seating but does not increase pitch.
fix: Write: wear of pins and bushes, which increases pitch and elongates the chain; separate roller wear and roller breakage as their own modes.

problem: The question asks for 'the four main parts' but the answer lists five items (pin, bush, roller, inner plates, outer plates).
fix: Ask for 'the parts of a roller chain link' and answer: pin, bush, roller, inner plate, outer plate; the roller touches the tooth.

problem: 'the pin is supported on one side' is not the real reason. In an offset (cranked) link the plate is offset, so the load path is eccentric and the plate is bent as well as pulled; that is why it is weak.
fix: Answer: the offset link uses a cranked plate, so the pull is eccentric and the plate carries bending on top of tension; it is the weakest link and a common failure point.

problem: The substitution writes ((19)/(2π))² where the symbol is ((Z₂ − Z₁)/(2π))². The number is right only because Z₂ − Z₁ happens to equal 19; a student copying the pattern with other tooth counts will get it wrong.

The factor of safety of 9.7 on breaking load looks comfortable, so a student may conclude the 08B chain is fine for 7.5 kW at 1000 rpm. Breaking-load FoS is not the selection check; the catalogue power rating, limited by plate fatigue and wear, governs, and a single-strand 08B is normally rated well below 7.5 kW at 1000 rpm.
fix: Add one line: this FoS only shows the chain will not break in tension; whether 08B is acceptable must be checked against its catalogue power rating at 1000 rpm with the service factor applied.

problem: 'The cost is chordal action: ... so speed pulses, the chain wears, and it must be lubricated' ties wear and the need for lubrication to chordal action. Wear comes from sliding at the pin-bush hinge under load; lubrication is needed for that hinge, not because of the polygon effect.
fix: Write: the cost is chordal action, which makes the speed pulse and adds impact at engagement; separately, the pin-bush hinge slides under load, so the chain must be lubricated and it wears as pitch elongates.

problem: 'the pitch-circle form is v = π d N/60' is unclear wording; students may not see why two formulas are given.
fix: Say: the exact mean chain speed from the polygon perimeter is v = Z₁ p N₁/60, while π d₁ N₁/60 is the speed of a point on the pitch circle; the two differ by less than 1% for Z ≥ 17.
